messages.subject_clean: [JIRA] (SPARKR-242) Failure in LR example
messages.body_plain:
Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui> commented on  SPARKR-242 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-242>

Re: Failure in LR example <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-242>

I have the same problem. This is caused by my PR: https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/214 for implemetation of zipRDD().

The key part is @ https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/214/files#diff-5da4cc93153d033022b481f9cbee4f06L55
data <- readLines(inputCon)
+ data <- as.list(readLines(inputCon))

Prior to this change, for RDDs from text files, a partition function will receive a charactor vector instead of a string list repsenting the string records within the partition. Since strSplit() works on a charactor vector, so LR example works well.

In the implemenation of zipRDD(), a partition length record is appended to each partition of the two source RDDs (https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/214/files#diff-374a93f8266cf295e710bc9676e2873bR1412). If any RDD is from text file, A numeric length appended to a character vector will be coerced to a character. Thus, at https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/214/files#diff-374a93f8266cf295e710bc9676e2873bR1429, A length is a charactor instead of numeric, which causes the subsequent operations fail.

I made the change in woker.R to solve this problem where a list of character instead of a character vector is passed to a partition function. Because list allows items of different types, a numeric length can be appended to a partition data list and retreived as a numeric. The other reason I made this change is that I think we should provide a consistent API to the user that a partition function will receive a list as partition data in all cases.

So to solve the issue reported in this JIRA, we have two options:
1. Roll back the change in worker.R. Which means, a partition func in some cases may receive a vector instead of a list. and user should be aware of this. And in zipRDD(), when a length is read, it should be coerced to a numeric in case it is a character.

2. Update the LR example readPartition() function to work on a string list.

folks, what's your opinion?

Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui> created an issue

SparkR <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR> /  <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-244> SPARKR-244 <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-244>
[SparkR-SQL] unit test failure after integration of PR that implements subtract() and subtractByKey() <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-244>
Issue Type:    Bug
Assignee:   Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui>
Created:   08/Apr/15 4:49 AM
Priority:    Major
Reporter:   Sun Rui <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/secure/ViewProfile.jspa?name=sunrui>

Test failure log:

1. Error: subtract() on RDDs ---------------------------------------------------
error in evaluating the argument 'x' in selecting a method for function 'collect':
unable to find an inherited method for function ‘subtract’ for signature ‘"RDD", "RDD"’
Calls: subtract -> <Anonymous>
1: withCallingHandlers(eval(code, new_test_environment), error = capture_calls)
2: eval(code, new_test_environment)
3: eval(expr, envir, enclos)
4: collect(subtract(rdd1, rdd1)) at test_rdd.R:459
5: .handleSimpleError(function (e)
Unknown macro: { e$calls <- head(sys.calls()[-seq_len(frame + 7)], -2) signalCondition(e) }

, "error in evaluating the argument 'x' in selecting a method for function 'collect': Error in (function (classes, fdef, mtable) : \n unable to find an inherited method for function ‘subtract’ for signature ‘\"RDD\", \"RDD\"’\nCalls: subtract -> <Anonymous>\n",
quote(collect(subtract(rdd1, rdd1))))
Error: Test failures
In addition: Warning message:
closing unused connection 5 (raw(0))
Execution halted
Had test failures; see logs.
The command "./run-tests.sh" exited with 255.

The cause is due to generic function name conflict. DF has a method called subtract, while RDD also has this method.

According to https://spark.apache.org/docs/1.3.0/api/scala/index.html#org.apache.spark.sql.DataFrame, DF has a method called except instead of subtract (which has the same functionality).

So it seems that changing DF.subtract to DF.except will solve this conflict. Does anyone know the reason why changing except to subtract before?

Re: [SparkR-SQL] unit test failure after integration of PR that implements subtract() and subtractByKey() <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-244>

Compared with DF.subtract, RDD.subtract has one more optional parameter numPartitions. Seems it is possible for them to share a single generic function. If there is no strong reason, keeping SparkR DF API consistent with DF scala API is of more importance, I think.

Re: [SparkR-SQL] unit test failure after integration of PR that implements subtract() and subtractByKey() <https://sparkr.atlassian.net/browse/SPARKR-244>

I think it's simply because 'except' is a reserved word in Python, so PySpark opted to use 'subtract' [1]. The SparkR API was probably implemented w.r.t. PySpark.

We should just go ahead and name it as 'except' in SparkR.

[1] https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/master/python/pyspark/sql/dataframe.py#L677

messages.subject: SparkR development updates
messages.subject_clean: SparkR development updates
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

The PR to integrate SparkR with mainline Spark was merged yesterday. As we shift our development into the Spark repository, I wanted to give an update of some things that will change

1. For PRs which are already in progress in the old repository or were recently merged, we will do a one bulk PR in Spark to sync things up.

2. We will update the README and other documentation in our old github repository to point users, developers to the Spark repository. As I mentioned in the previous email in the old repository the master branch will support Spark versions <= 1.2 and the sparkr-sql branch will be named as branch-1.3 and will support Spark 1.3.

3. We will export all open issues from the existing JIRA and migrate it to the Spark JIRA [1] under the component 'SparkR'. We will then place the old JIRA in maintenance mode (i.e. the existing issues will still be available, but new issues should be created in the Spark JIRA).

4. New pull requests for features and bug fixes should be sent to the Spark repository from now. In the Spark development process (documented here [2]), we will create a JIRA issue for every PR and use [SPARKR] in the PR title.

5. We will ensure that all major bug fixes for bugs already reported and new bug fixes which affect the code in the old repository will be back-ported.

Finally, I'd eventually like to shift discussions about SparkR from this mailing list to the Spark user/dev mailing list (http://spark.apache.org/community.html). We'll keep this list active a for some time and I'll send another update before we make changes to it.

Please let me know if you have any questions / clarifications and thanks for your patience and help with this transition.

Thanks
Shivaram

[1] https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK
[2] https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/SPARK/Contributing+to+Spark

Hi Srikanth,

If you are looking for an experimental SparkR streaming, you may take a look at https://github.com/hlin09/spark/tree/SparkR-streaming. A standalone version compatible with previous Spark versions are also available at https://github.com/hlin09/SparkR-pkg/tree/SparkR-streaming/.

Thanks,

Hao

On Thursday, March 19, 2015 at 8:39:50 PM UTC-4, Srikanth wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> It was great to see SparkR treated as first class citizen during Spark Summit East talks.
> I wanted to check if there is any plans of supporting Spark's streaming with R? I see there is jira ticket open with no updates.
>
> My requirement is to use a model developed in R on a stream of incoming input. I don't really need to have streaming context accessed in R. Its more like a Storm Bolt written in R.
> I want to avoid starting R process for each block. Do you have any thoughts on having a "R process" per worker that can take input, apply a function and return output? Something like Rserve may be??
>
> Thanks,
> Srikanth
>

messages.body_plain:
Zongheng,

I would say it is at very early stage as experimental branch, only used internally in some analytics application as research project. It would be good to see how much it could benefit the community, as I also submitted an issue as https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SPARK-6803.

On Thursday, April 9, 2015 at 6:20:25 PM UTC-4, Zongheng Yang wrote:
> Hao,
>
> This is great stuff.  What's the status of your branch?
>
> On Thu, Apr 9, 2015 at 3:18 PM hlin09 <hlin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Srikanth,
> >
> > If you are looking for an experimental SparkR streaming, you may take a look at https://github.com/hlin09/spark/tree/SparkR-streaming. A standalone version compatible with previous Spark versions are also available at https://github.com/hlin09/SparkR-pkg/tree/SparkR-streaming/.
> >
> > Thanks,
> >
> > Hao
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, March 19, 2015 at 8:39:50 PM UTC-4, Srikanth wrote:
> > > Hi all,
> > >
> > > It was great to see SparkR treated as first class citizen during Spark Summit East talks.
> > > I wanted to check if there is any plans of supporting Spark's streaming with R? I see there is jira ticket open with no updates.
> > >
> > > My requirement is to use a model developed in R on a stream of incoming input. I don't really need to have streaming context accessed in R. Its more like a Storm Bolt written in R.
> > > I want to avoid starting R process for each block. Do you have any thoughts on having a "R process" per worker that can take input, apply a function and return output? Something like Rserve may be??
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > > Srikanth

> 1. The cache on textFile works a little differently in SparkR vs. PySpark.
> In SparkR we cache JavaRDD encoded as strings, while Python encodes it in
> Python. The reason this is important is that Strings in Java take 2 bytes
> per character vs 1 byte in most other languages. So one workaround in your
> case is to cache an R encoded RDD by explicitly calling `lapply`. i.e. You
> can do "lines <- cache(lapply(textFile(sc, <filepath>), identity))" -- This
> halves the cached dataset size from what I observed (i.e. each partition is
> down from 1G to 500 MB)
>
> 2. I also found that in this case calling `strsplit` is slow and you
> probably don't want to do that every time. So another optimization could be
> to do `strsplit` before cache.

> >
> > 1. The cache on textFile works a little differently in SparkR vs. PySpark.
> > In SparkR we cache JavaRDD encoded as strings, while Python encodes it in
> > Python. The reason this is important is that Strings in Java take 2 bytes
> > per character vs 1 byte in most other languages. So one workaround in your
> > case is to cache an R encoded RDD by explicitly calling `lapply`. i.e. You
> > can do "lines <- cache(lapply(textFile(sc, <filepath>), identity))" -- This
> > halves the cached dataset size from what I observed (i.e. each partition is
> > down from 1G to 500 MB)
> >
> > 2. I also found that in this case calling `strsplit` is slow and you
> > probably don't want to do that every time. So another optimization could be
> > to do `strsplit` before cache.
> >
> > 3. Finally we've recently merged a PR that removes the dependency on rJava.
> > So you can skip that step during the installation process. I'll update the
> > SparkR wiki soon.

messages.body_plain:
One more followup on this.

I tried to use repartition with the same airline dataset used earlier
in this thread. And I got the same error as in the previous message in
this thread.

Here's the code I ran:

hdfs_master <- system("cat /root/ephemeral-hdfs/conf/masters", intern = TRUE)
lines <- textFile(sc, paste0("hdfs://", hdfs_master, ":9000/data/airline"))

linesPartitioned <- repartition(lines, numPartitions = as.integer(96))
count(linesPartitioned)

Note that the same error occurs when I use a much smaller version of
the dataset, just the first three of the 22 original files. This
smaller dataset around 1 Gb.

-chris

>>> > Thanks a lot for posting the data and the code -- I used this to do a

>>> > of debugging and profiling today (but this was on a cluster with more
>>> > memory). I've opened a PR with some fixes I made at
>>> > https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg/pull/147
>>> >
>>> > 1. The cache on textFile works a little differently in SparkR vs.
>>> > PySpark.
>>> > In SparkR we cache JavaRDD encoded as strings, while Python encodes it
>>> > in
>>> > Python. The reason this is important is that Strings in Java take 2
>>> > bytes
>>> > per character vs 1 byte in most other languages. So one workaround in
>>> > your
>>> > case is to cache an R encoded RDD by explicitly calling `lapply`. i.e.
>>> > You
>>> > can do "lines <- cache(lapply(textFile(sc, <filepath>), identity))" --
>>> > This
>>> > halves the cached dataset size from what I observed (i.e. each partition
>>> > is
>>> > down from 1G to 500 MB)
>>> >
>>> > 2. I also found that in this case calling `strsplit` is slow and you
>>> > probably don't want to do that every time. So another optimization could
>>> > be
>>> > to do `strsplit` before cache.
>>> >
>>> > 3. Finally we've recently merged a PR that removes the dependency on
>>> > rJava.
>>> > So you can skip that step during the installation process. I'll update
>>> > the
>>> > SparkR wiki soon.
>>> >
>>> > Shivaram

>>> >> ":9000/data/airline")))
>>> >> count(lines)
>>> >> take(lines, 5)
>>> >>
>>> >> sfo_lines = filterRDD(lines, function(line) strsplit(line,
>>> >> ",")[[1]][17] == "SFO")
>>> >> count(sfo_lines)
>>> >>
>>> >> createKeyValue <- function(line) {
>>> >>     vals = strsplit(line, ",")[[1]]
>>> >>     return(list(paste(vals[17], vals[18], sep = '+'), 1))
>>> >>   }
>>> >>
>>> >> routeCount <- collect(reduceByKey(map(lines, createKeyValue), "+", 1L))
>>> >> routeCount2 <- countByKey(map(lines, createKeyValue))
>>> >>
>>> >> Also, once I start up the EC2 cluster and am logged in, here is how I
>>> >> set up SparkR:
>>> >>
>>> >> echo '#!/bin/bash' > /usr/bin/realpath
>>> >> echo 'readlink -e $1' >> /usr/bin/realpath
>>> >> chmod guo+x /usr/bin/realpath

>>> >> R CMD javareconf
>>> >> tar xvzf rJava_0.9-6.tar.gz; R CMD INSTALL rJava
>>> >> /root/spark-ec2/copy-dir /usr/bin/realpath
>>> >> /root/spark/sbin/slaves.sh R CMD javareconf
>>> >> /root/spark/sbin/slaves.sh R CMD INSTALL ~/rJava_0.9-6.tar.gz
>>> >>
>>> >> cd /root
>>> >> git clone https://github.com/amplab-extras/SparkR-pkg.git
>>> >> cd SparkR-pkg
>>> >> SPARK_VERSION=1.1.0 ./install-dev.sh
>>> >> /root/spark-ec2/copy-dir /root/SparkR-pkg
>>> >>
>>> >> # read data into HDFS:
>>> >> mkdir /mnt/airline
>>> >> cd /mnt/airline
>>> >> wget http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/share/paciorek/1987-2008.csvs.tgz
>>> >> tar -xvzf 1987-2008.csvs.tgz
>>> >> export PATH=$PATH:/root/ephemeral-hdfs/bin/
>>> >> hadoop fs -mkdir /data/airline
>>> >> hadoop fs -copyFromLocal /mnt/airline/*bz2 /data/airline
>>> >> hadoop fs -ls /data/airline
>>> >>
>>> >>
>>> >> # start SparkR
>>> >> cd /root/SparkR-pkg
>>> >> MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR
>>> >>
>>> >>

>>> >> >> > Replies in line
>>> >> >> >
>>> >> >> >
>>> >> >> > On Fri, Jan 16, 2015 at 12:02 PM, Chris Paciorek
>>> >> >> > <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> Ok, I've done some more exploration. Sorry for the dense post,
>>> >> >> >> but
>>> >> >> >> hopefully the detail will be helpful.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> Here's the setting. I'm using Spark 1.1.0. Original dataset is
>>> >> >> >> about
>>> >> >> >> 12 Gb as flat text, less when on the HDFS in bz2 format. It's
>>> >> >> >> split
>>> >> >> >> into 22 .bz2 files on the HDFS and while not wildly different in

>>> >> >> >> there is some variation in size across the files. I'm using a
>>> >> >> >> 12-worker EC2 cluster, each worker has 2 cores and 7.6 Gb RAM.
>>> >> >> >> I'm
>>> >> >> >> calling SparkR as:
>>> >> >> >> MASTER=`cat /root/spark-ec2/cluster-url` SPARK_MEM=6g ./sparkR
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> I then do sc.textFile to read in and do filterRDD and
>>> >> >> >> map/reduceByKey
>>> >> >> >> operations.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> When I do cache the original dataset, I see about 1.3 Gb memory
>>> >> >> >> per
>>> >> >> >> partition, and most of the nodes use up to 2.7 Gb as they have 2
>>> >> >> >> partitions assigned (a couple nodes only have one of the 22
>>> >> >> >> partitions, so use less memory).
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> First a couple background questions:
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> 1)  I'd expect 6 Gb available on each worker, so 6 Gb per
>>> >> >> >> executor.
>>> >> >> >> However both in SparkR and when I invoke PySpark without setting
>>> >> >> >> SPARK_MEM, I see in the UI that each executor has 3 Gb available.
>>> >> >> >> Can
>>> >> >> >> anyone clarify where the other 3 Gb is?
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> > 6 Gb is the total memory given to the Spark executor. Of that only
>>> >> >> > 60%
>>> >> >> > is
>>> >> >> > used for caching. The rest of the memory is used as scratch space
>>> >> >> > during
>>> >> >> > computation. The UI only shows memory used / available for
>>> >> >> > caching.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> 2) In the UI, I see 12 executors and often see 2 active tasks per
>>> >> >> >> executor, which makes sense. But Shivaram suggested using fewer
>>> >> >> >> executors. When I change SPARK_WORKER_CORES, I still see 12
>>> >> >> >> executors,
>>> >> >> >> but only 1 active task per executor, which makes sense to me
>>> >> >> >> given
>>> >> >> >> each node has 2 cores, but seems not to be what Shivaram was
>>> >> >> >> suggesting.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >  So SPARK_WORKER_CORES controls the number of parallel threads
>>> >> >> > used
>>> >> >> > on a
>>> >> >> > executor and thus controls the number of active tasks. If we set
>>> >> >> > it
>>> >> >> > to
>>> >> >> > 1,
>>> >> >> > there will be 1 active task at a time and this was what I was
>>> >> >> > suggesting
>>> >> >> > before.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> Now some results from trying with and without caching and
>>> >> >> >> reducing
>>> >> >> >> SPARK_WORKER_CORES to 1.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> Case A: My original attempt, with SPARK_WORKER_CORES=2 and with
>>> >> >> >> caching. This causes the executor failure mentioned in the
>>> >> >> >> previous
>>> >> >> >> thread.  I am able to cache the initial dataset but then
>>> >> >> >> subsequent
>>> >> >> >> operations lead to the failure. I note that there are a couple
>>> >> >> >> nodes
>>> >> >> >> with 2.7 Gb or so used by the RDD partitions on those nodes. So
>>> >> >> >> an
>>> >> >> >> out
>>> >> >> >> of memory problem seems plausible given the availability of only
>>> >> >> >> 3
>>> >> >> >> Gb
>>> >> >> >> rather than 6 Gb.  That said, shouldn't Spark/SparkR be robust to
>>> >> >> >> this
>>> >> >> >> and automatically fall back to disk instead of failing
>>> >> >> >> catastrophically?
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >
>>> >> >> > SparkR doesn't yet have support for spilling to disk in the middle
>>> >> >> > of
>>> >> >> > a
>>> >> >> > computation.  It assumes that an entire partition of input can be
>>> >> >> > loaded
>>> >> >> > into R and processed.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> As noted, PySpark handles this dataset and analogous operations
>>> >> >> >> just
>>> >> >> >> fine with caching.
>>> >> >> >> When I look at memory used by the RDD for PySpark, the maximum on
>>> >> >> >> any
>>> >> >> >> given node is 500 Mb.
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> >> So this presumably explains why PySpark is fine. But are the
>>> >> >> >> underlying data structures different for PySpark and SparkR? I
>>> >> >> >> thought
>>> >> >> >> both had the data in memory in Java on the back end?
>>> >> >> >>
>>> >> >> > The data in the backend is stored in a serialized format (Java
>>> >> >> > just
>>> >> >> > seems it
>>> >> >> > as byte array). The format is different for each language and in
>>> >> >> > SparkR
>>> >> >> > we
>>> >> >> > use the `serialize` command in R to serialize data. It could very
>>> >> >> > well
>>> >> >> > be
>>> >> >> > that R's format is more inefficient than Python here.
>>> >> >> >

messages.subject: Re: Is auto.arima() can be done using sparkR
messages.subject_clean: Is auto.arima() can be done using sparkR
messages.body_plain:
SparkR does not support auto.arima out of the box, but I guess it can be implemented using SparkR if you are aware of a way to parallelize the computation.

Regarding R libraries, typically you can use existing R libraries inside functions being executed on the executors.
P.S: Now that SparkR has been merged with mainline Spark, you can send SparkR related questions to us...@spark.apache.org

Thanks
Shivaram

Shivaram
